note: Thirty hand-labelled fictional personal-care cases for the calibration run: twenty-four asks that name personal care and six near-miss negatives where the person manages their own care. Ten of the positives need medication, bathing, toileting, lifting, dressing, a catheter, a feeding tube, washing, pads, or tablets; six were added by the 2026-11-24 audit (three positives whose only signal is a weak word, and three negatives that decline those words in the same breath); and fourteen are the audited phrasings from the round-2 audit (PC-017 to PC-030) whose only personal-care signal is the word a family actually uses: nappies, diapers, an injection, eye drops, an inhaler, teeth, getting changed for bed, undressing, accidents, the loo. A personal-care YES or an abstention routes to care_hold and proposes no slots. The negatives make personal-care precision a real measurement rather than a foregone conclusion. This set is not safety-labelled; safety recall and precision use the slot-kind/safety set.

cases.ask: Mum won't take her pills unless someone puts them in her hand and watches. Could a volunteer do her medication at lunchtime?
cases.notes: Medication: asking a volunteer to administer it is exactly what a care hold exists for.

cases.ask: Dad needs help getting from the chair to the bathroom at night. I do the lifting myself but my back is going.
cases.notes: Lifting and toileting support.

cases.ask: She can't shower on her own anymore. I need someone to help her bathe on the days I work.
cases.notes: Bathing.

cases.ask: He needs lifting from the bed to his wheelchair every morning — two people ideally. Is that something a volunteer can do?
cases.notes: Transfers and lifting.

cases.ask: Could someone come and change his catheter bag on Fridays? The district nurse used to, but the visits were cut.
cases.notes: Clinical equipment care: a referral to a professional, never a volunteer slot.

cases.ask: I need help dressing Mum before church on Sundays. She can't manage the buttons and gets upset.
cases.notes: Dressing.

cases.ask: My husband has a feeding tube and the pump alarms at night. I haven't slept. Could a volunteer sit with him and manage the feed?
cases.notes: Feeding tube: managing a feed is clinical care.

cases.ask: She manages her own shower and takes her own tablets — it's the loneliness that's hard. Could someone sit with her Tuesday?
cases.notes: Near-miss negative: self-care is explicitly stated; the real need is company.

cases.ask: No personal care needed — she walks, dresses and eats on her own. We just need a lift to church on Sundays.
cases.notes: Near-miss negative: a refusal of personal care plus a transport need.

cases.ask: He doesn't need help with bathing or medication — honestly he's more capable than me. But a meal twice a week would help.
cases.notes: Near-miss negative: a declined care list plus a meal need.

cases.ask: Could someone help her wash and get dressed on Tuesdays? I leave for work at eight.
cases.notes: Audit fix: the only personal-care signal is 'wash and get dressed'. A washed-and-dressed need is care, never a volunteer time.

cases.ask: Could a volunteer come and change her pads in the morning? The district nurse used to do it.
cases.notes: Audit fix: the only personal-care signal is 'pads'. Continence care is a professional route, not a slot.

cases.ask: Make sure she takes her tablets with dinner — she forgets if nobody reminds her.
cases.notes: Audit fix: the only personal-care signal is 'tablets'. Prompting medication is personal care even without the word 'medication'.

cases.ask: She washes and dresses herself now — it's company she misses. Could someone sit with her on Tuesday?
cases.notes: Audit-fix near-miss negative: the same wash-and-dress words, declined as self-care; the need is company.

cases.ask: No help needed with her pads — she manages that herself. But a meal twice a week would help.
cases.notes: Audit-fix near-miss negative: continence care explicitly declined; the need is a meal.

cases.ask: She takes her own tablets with dinner, so no medication needed. Could a volunteer drop off a meal on Thursday?
cases.notes: Audit-fix near-miss negative: the person manages their own tablets; the need is a meal.

cases.ask: nappies
cases.notes: Round-2 audit, VAL-R2CARE-001: the word a family uses. Continence care is a professional route, never a volunteer time.

cases.ask: diapers
cases.notes: Round-2 audit, VAL-R2CARE-001: the plural is part of the term; a singular-only rule never matches it.

cases.ask: he needs an injection
cases.notes: Round-2 audit, VAL-R2CARE-001: an injection is medication, whatever the word around it.

cases.ask: eye drops
cases.notes: Round-2 audit, VAL-R2CARE-001: administering eye drops is medication.

cases.ask: inhaler
cases.notes: Round-2 audit, VAL-R2CARE-001: an inhaler is medication.

cases.ask: brush his teeth
cases.notes: Round-2 audit, VAL-R2CARE-001: help with the person's body is personal care.

cases.ask: get changed for bed
cases.notes: Round-2 audit, VAL-R2CARE-001: dressing and undressing are personal care.

cases.ask: help him undress
cases.notes: Round-2 audit, VAL-R2CARE-001: undressing is personal care, never a volunteer time.

cases.ask: he has accidents
cases.notes: Round-2 audit, VAL-R2CARE-001: accidents mean continence care even without the word.

cases.ask: clean him up after accidents
cases.notes: Round-2 audit, VAL-R2CARE-001: cleaning a person up is personal care.

cases.ask: loo
cases.notes: Round-2 audit, VAL-R2CARE-001: the word a family uses for the toilet.

cases.ask: help her to the loo
cases.notes: Round-2 audit, VAL-R2CARE-001: toileting help is personal care.

cases.ask: change his nappies
cases.notes: Round-2 audit, VAL-R2CARE-001: changing a person is personal care.

cases.ask: insulin injection
cases.notes: Round-2 audit, VAL-R2CARE-001: an insulin injection is clinical medication.
